title: Absolute and relative poverty
overview: Poverty is not one thing: absolute poverty is about whether people can meet basic needs, while relative poverty is about how far people fall behind the typical living standard of their own society. Edexcel expects you to define and measure both precisely, explain their causes in the UK and in developing economies, and analyse why each can move in a different direction over time. This topic underpins Paper 2 and Paper 3 questions on growth, inequality, development and fiscal policy.
objectives: Distinguish absolute from relative poverty and explain how each is measured in the UK and globally
Calculate a relative poverty line and explain equivalisation and before/after housing costs measures
Explain the causes of poverty in the UK and in developing economies with chains of reasoning
Analyse why absolute and relative poverty can change in different directions over time
Evaluate policies to reduce poverty, including the National Living Wage and the benefit system

sections.heading: Absolute poverty: can people meet basic needs?
sections.body:
**Absolute poverty** exists when a household's income is too low to buy the minimum bundle of goods needed for survival and basic functioning: food, clean water, shelter, clothing, sanitation and basic healthcare. The key feature is that the threshold is fixed in real terms. It does not move when average incomes rise, so sustained economic growth that reaches the poor will reduce absolute poverty.

The best-known global measure is the World Bank's **international poverty line** of extreme poverty. Since its 2025 update this is $3.00 a day per person, measured in 2021 purchasing power parity (PPP) dollars (it was previously $2.15 a day in 2017 PPP). PPP conversion matters: $3.00 converted at market exchange rates would buy far more in Ethiopia than in the USA, so PPP rates adjust for differences in price levels. The World Bank also publishes higher lines (around $4.20 and $8.30 a day) that are more relevant to lower-middle and upper-middle income countries.

Income lines miss many deprivations. The UNDP and Oxford's **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)** counts a person as poor if they are deprived in at least a third of ten weighted indicators across health (nutrition, child mortality), education (years of schooling, school attendance) and living standards (cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets). Around 1.1 billion people were classed as multidimensionally poor in recent UNDP reports, a larger number than extreme income poverty, which shows that rising income alone does not guarantee access to services.

The UK also publishes an official **absolute poverty** measure: the share of people living in households with income below 60% of the 2010/11 median, held constant in real terms. Note the trap: this is still an income threshold, but it is frozen in real terms, so it behaves like an absolute measure.

sections.heading: Relative poverty: falling behind your own society
sections.body:
**Relative poverty** exists when a household's income is so far below the typical income in that society that its members cannot participate in normal activities (school trips, a mobile phone contract, heating the whole home). The UK and EU standard measure is household income below **60% of the contemporary median equivalised household income**.

Three technical features earn credit:
- **Median, not mean.** The median is the income of the middle household, so it is not dragged upwards by a few very high earners.
- **Equivalisation.** A household of two adults and two children needs more income than a single adult to reach the same living standard, but not four times as much because of shared housing and bills. Incomes are adjusted using an equivalence scale so different household types can be compared.
- **Before housing costs (BHC) and after housing costs (AHC).** AHC deducts rent or mortgage interest. Because poorer households, especially renters in London, spend a large share of income on housing, AHC poverty rates are higher; around a fifth of the UK population and roughly 30% of children are in relative poverty on the AHC measure in recent Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) data.

Because the line moves with the median, relative poverty is really a measure of inequality in the lower half of the distribution. In a recession, if median income falls faster than benefit incomes, measured relative poverty can fall even though nobody is better off; this happened in the UK after 2008. Conversely, rapid growth that raises the median faster than low incomes increases relative poverty even when every household is better off in real terms.

Other useful UK indicators include **persistent poverty** (in relative poverty in at least three of the last four years), **material deprivation** (unable to afford items such as a winter coat or keeping the home warm) and **destitution** (unable to afford essentials such as food and heating), tracked by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation.

sections.heading: Causes of poverty in the UK
sections.body:
A strong answer explains a cause as a chain: cause, mechanism, effect on household income relative to needs.

- **Unemployment and economic inactivity.** Losing a job cuts income to benefit levels, which in the UK are set well below the relative poverty line for most household types. Long-term sickness has become a major driver of inactivity since the pandemic.
- **Low pay and in-work poverty.** Around seven in ten children in poverty live in a household where at least one adult works. Low hourly pay, part-time hours, zero-hours contracts and insecure self-employment mean work does not guarantee escape from poverty.
- **The tax and benefit system.** Real-terms benefit freezes (2016 to 2020), the benefit cap and the two-child limit on Universal Credit and Child Tax Credit (introduced in 2017, and which the government announced in 2025 it would remove) reduced incomes of larger low-income families. Pensioner poverty fell sharply over recent decades partly because the state pension has been protected by the triple lock since 2011.
- **The poverty trap.** As earnings rise, Universal Credit is withdrawn at a taper rate of 55% of net earnings, on top of income tax and National Insurance. This creates very high **effective marginal tax rates**, weakening the incentive to work extra hours.
- **Housing costs.** High rents relative to incomes, particularly in London and the South East, explain why AHC poverty is much higher than BHC poverty.
- **Household characteristics.** Lone-parent families, larger families, households with a disabled member, some ethnic minority groups and people with low qualifications face higher poverty risk.
- **Inflation.** Poorer households spend a larger share of income on food and energy. When CPI inflation peaked at around 11% in late 2022, driven by energy and food, the real incomes of low-income households were squeezed hardest.

sections.heading: Causes of poverty in developing economies
sections.body:
In low-income countries the key issue is low **productivity**, which keeps incomes close to subsistence.

- **Dependence on subsistence agriculture.** A large share of the workforce farms small plots with little capital, so output per worker is low and highly exposed to weather and climate shocks such as drought.
- **Low human capital.** Limited schooling and poor health (malaria, malnutrition, stunting) reduce productivity and earnings for life; poor children become poor adults, a **cycle of poverty**.
- **Weak institutions and conflict.** Corruption, insecure property rights and civil war destroy capital and deter investment. Conflict-affected states now account for a rising share of the world's extreme poor.
- **Lack of access to credit.** Without collateral or formal banking, the poor cannot borrow to invest in seeds, livestock or a small business.
- **Primary product dependency and volatile prices.** Falling commodity prices cut export earnings and rural incomes.
- **Rapid population growth.** A high dependency ratio spreads household income across more people.

Geography matters. Most of the people in extreme poverty now live in sub-Saharan Africa, whereas in 1990 the majority lived in East and South Asia. China's rapid growth after 1978 lifted close to 800 million people out of extreme poverty, according to the World Bank, which shows the power of sustained growth combined with rising labour demand in manufacturing.

sections.heading: Why poverty changes over time
sections.body:
Absolute and relative poverty respond differently to the same events, and examiners reward students who spot this.

- **Economic growth.** If real incomes rise across the distribution, absolute poverty falls. Relative poverty falls only if incomes of the poorest grow faster than the median. Global extreme poverty fell from over a third of the world's population in 1990 to under a tenth before the pandemic, mainly due to growth in Asia.
- **Recessions and shocks.** Covid-19 pushed global extreme poverty up in 2020 for the first time in decades. In the UK, furlough and the temporary £20-a-week Universal Credit uplift cushioned incomes, so relative poverty did not rise as much as many feared.
- **Inflation and the cost of living.** High inflation that outpaces benefits and wages raises absolute poverty; relative poverty may change little if the median falls in real terms too.
- **Policy choices.** Generous transfers, higher minimum wages and free services (school meals, childcare) reduce poverty; freezes and caps raise it.
- **Structural change.** Automation and globalisation can reduce demand for low-skilled labour, raising poverty in regions dependent on declining industries, while creating jobs elsewhere.
- **Demography.** An ageing population with protected pensions shifts poverty away from pensioners and towards families with children.

sections.heading: Policies to reduce poverty and their limits
sections.body:
**National Living Wage (NLW).** The NLW for workers aged 21 and over was £12.21 an hour from April 2025, with the long-run aim of reaching two-thirds of median hourly earnings. It raises hourly pay for the lowest paid, but most poor households are poor because of too few hours or no work, so its effect on household poverty is diluted. If the wage floor is set above the equilibrium wage, the classical model predicts some unemployment, though UK evidence since 1999 has found little job loss so far, partly because employers have monopsony power in low-pay labour markets.

**Benefits.** Raising Universal Credit or child-related payments targets poor households directly and quickly. The trade-offs are cost, possible disincentive effects and, if withdrawal is steep, a deeper poverty trap. Lowering the taper rate improves work incentives but extends benefits further up the income scale, raising cost.

**Education and skills.** Raising human capital tackles the root cause of low pay, but benefits come with a long time lag and depend on quality.

**Developing economies.** Conditional cash transfers (Brazil's Bolsa Família, Mexico's Progresa), employment guarantees (India's rural employment scheme), microfinance and investment in health and infrastructure all target the poor. Their success depends on governance, targeting and whether growth creates productive jobs.

key_terms.definition: A situation in which household income is insufficient to buy the minimum goods and services needed for basic survival and functioning; the threshold is fixed in real terms.
A situation in which household income is below a set proportion of typical income in that society; in the UK, below 60% of contemporary median equivalised household income.
The World Bank threshold for extreme poverty, $3.00 a day per person in 2021 PPP dollars since 2025.
An exchange rate adjusted so that a given amount of money buys the same basket of goods in each country, allowing real living standards to be compared.
Adjusting household income for household size and composition so that the living standards of different household types can be compared.
A measure of income after deducting rent, mortgage interest and other housing costs; gives a better picture of disposable living standards where housing is expensive.
Poverty experienced by households in which at least one adult is in paid employment.
A situation where the combined effect of benefit withdrawal and taxes on extra earnings leaves people little better off, weakening incentives to work more.
The proportion of an extra pound of gross earnings lost through taxes and reduced benefits.
Deprivation across several dimensions such as health, education and living standards, rather than income alone, as measured by the MPI.
Being in relative poverty in the current year and in at least two of the previous three years.
A self-reinforcing process in which low income leads to poor health and education, which keeps productivity and future income low, often across generations.

diagrams.title: Income distribution and the relative poverty line
diagrams.caption: Household incomes are right-skewed, so the median lies below the mean. Households to the left of 60% of the median are in relative poverty. If every income doubled, the whole distribution and both lines would move right together, leaving relative poverty unchanged while absolute poverty fell.

diagrams.title: National Living Wage in a competitive low-pay labour market
diagrams.caption: A wage floor above We raises pay for the Qd workers who keep their jobs, reducing in-work poverty, but in a competitive market employment falls from Qe to Qd and Qs minus Qd workers are unemployed. Under monopsony the floor can raise both wages and employment, which is why the size of any job losses is an empirical question.

formulae.name: Relative poverty line
formulae.formula: 0.6 × median equivalised household income
formulae.example: If median equivalised household income is £36,000 a year (illustrative), the relative poverty line is 0.6 × 36,000 = £21,600. A household on £20,000 is in relative poverty. If all incomes rise by 10%, the median becomes £39,600 and the line £23,760; the household now earns £22,000, still below the line, so relative poverty is unchanged even though real income has risen.

formulae.name: Annual value of the international poverty line
formulae.formula: $ per day × 365 (PPP dollars)
formulae.example: $3.00 × 365 = $1,095 a year per person in 2021 PPP dollars. A family of five needs roughly $5,475 a year at PPP to be above the line.

formulae.name: Effective marginal tax rate (EMTR)
formulae.formula: (extra tax + extra NI + benefit withdrawn) ÷ extra gross earnings
formulae.example: A Universal Credit claimant paying 20% income tax and 8% NI earns an extra £100. Tax and NI take £28, leaving £72 net. UC is withdrawn at 55% of net earnings: 0.55 × 72 = £39.60. Total lost = 28 + 39.60 = £67.60, so the EMTR is 67.6% and the worker keeps only £32.40.

applications: UK child poverty: on the after-housing-costs measure roughly three in ten UK children have been in relative poverty in recent DWP data, around 4 million or more. Larger families were hit by the two-child limit introduced in 2017; the government announced in 2025 that it would be removed, a policy that independent analysts expected to be one of the most cost-effective ways of cutting child poverty because it targets large low-income families directly.

Cost-of-living crisis 2022 to 2023: CPI inflation peaked at around 11% in October 2022. Because energy and food take a larger share of poorer households' budgets, their personal inflation rates were higher than average. The government responded with the Energy Price Guarantee and targeted cost-of-living payments to means-tested benefit recipients, which limited the rise in absolute poverty.

National Living Wage: raised to £12.21 an hour for those aged 21 and over in April 2025, among the highest minimum wages relative to median pay in advanced economies. The Low Pay Commission has found limited evidence of job losses so far, but hospitality and retail employers have responded partly by cutting hours, which matters for household poverty.

China and India: World Bank estimates suggest China lifted close to 800 million people out of extreme poverty after 1978 through export-led manufacturing growth, rural reform and infrastructure. India has also reduced extreme poverty substantially, while relative poverty and inequality have risen, a clear case of absolute and relative measures diverging.

Sub-Saharan Africa: most of the world's extreme poor now live in the region. Rapid population growth, conflict (for example in Sudan), climate shocks and dependence on low-productivity agriculture mean that GDP growth of 3 to 4% a year has translated into slow reductions in poverty per person.
evaluation: Which measure? A policy can reduce absolute poverty while increasing relative poverty, or vice versa; a top-band answer states which measure it is judging and why that measure matters for the question.

Growth is necessary but not sufficient: the poverty impact of growth depends on its distribution (labour-intensive sectors and rural growth reduce poverty faster) and on whether governments use extra tax revenue for transfers and public services.

Measurement limits: income surveys under-record informal income, PPP estimates are revised, and a household just above the line is barely better off than one just below, so changes in headcount rates can overstate or understate real changes in hardship.
Time period: cash transfers cut poverty immediately, but education and health investment reduce poverty with a long lag and are more likely to be permanent.

Trade-offs: generous benefits reduce poverty but steep withdrawal rates create a poverty trap and cost the government money; minimum wages target workers rather than poor households and risk some unemployment if set too high.
Context: in the UK the main drivers are housing costs, family size and low hours, whereas in low-income countries they are low productivity and lack of services, so the most effective policy differs.
misconceptions: Relative poverty can never be eliminated. Wrong: if nobody has an income below 60% of the median, relative poverty is zero. It is a measure of the bottom of the distribution, not the bottom 20% of households.
Economic growth always reduces relative poverty. Growth raises the median, so relative poverty falls only if the incomes of the poor grow faster than the median.
People in poverty are mostly unemployed. In the UK most children in poverty live in working households; low hours and low pay are central causes.
Absolute poverty does not exist in the UK. The UK publishes an absolute poverty measure, and destitution, where people cannot afford food or heating, has risen in recent years.
Poverty is measured using mean income. The UK uses the median, which is not distorted by very high earners.
exam_tips: Always define the measure precisely: 60% of median equivalised household income for relative poverty; a fixed real threshold such as $3.00 a day at PPP for absolute poverty.
In data-response questions, check whether the extract uses BHC or AHC and whether figures are rates or numbers of people; a rising number can coincide with a falling rate when population grows.
Use a simple calculation to show why growth may leave relative poverty unchanged; it is quick, precise analysis that examiners reward.
Link causes to policies synoptically: the NLW (Theme 3 labour markets), benefits and taxes (4.5.2), growth (2.5) and development strategies (4.3.3).
For evaluation, distinguish between short-run income support and long-run measures that raise productivity, and consider the government budget constraint.

model_answer.question: Evaluate the likely effectiveness of increases in the National Living Wage as a policy to reduce relative poverty in the UK.
model_answer.answer:
The National Living Wage (NLW) is a legal minimum hourly wage for workers aged 21 and over, set at £12.21 an hour from April 2025. Relative poverty in the UK is defined as household income below 60% of contemporary median equivalised household income. The question is whether raising the wage floor lifts household incomes at the bottom of the distribution relative to the median.

The direct effect is clear. Low-paid workers in sectors such as retail, hospitality and social care receive a higher hourly wage. A full-time worker on 37.5 hours gains around £37.50 a week for each £1 rise in the hourly rate. Because the NLW is set relative to median earnings (the target of two-thirds of median hourly pay), it raises the lowest wages faster than the median wage, compressing the bottom of the earnings distribution. For a single adult working full time, this can move household income above 60% of the median, so relative poverty falls. There may also be spillover effects, as employers raise wages for workers just above the NLW to preserve pay differentials.

However, the policy may be less effective than it first appears. First, relative poverty is measured at the household level, not the individual level. Many NLW workers are second earners in households that are not poor, while many poor households contain no one in work, or someone working few hours. Around seven in ten poor children live in working households, but often the problem is too few hours rather than too low an hourly rate, so the NLW is poorly targeted at household poverty. Second, higher earnings trigger the Universal Credit taper: a claimant paying basic-rate tax and NI loses 55% of extra net earnings, so an extra £100 of gross pay raises income by only about £32. Much of the gain flows back to the Treasury rather than to the household.

Third, there may be employment effects. As shown on a labour market diagram, if the NLW is set above the equilibrium wage, the quantity of labour demanded falls from Qe to Qd, creating unemployment. A worker who loses their job falls to benefit income, which is far below the poverty line, increasing poverty. The evidence so far suggests job losses have been small, partly because many low-pay employers have monopsony power, where a minimum wage can raise both pay and employment. But as the NLW rises towards two-thirds of median earnings, and following the 2025 rise in employer National Insurance, firms may respond by cutting hours, freezing hiring or automating, which matters for household incomes even without outright job losses.

Finally, the effect depends on what happens to the median. If the NLW raises low wages faster than the median, relative poverty falls; but if other income sources, such as benefits, are frozen in real terms, poor households without work fall further behind.

On balance, NLW increases are likely to reduce in-work relative poverty modestly for single earners and full-time workers, but they are a blunt tool for reducing household relative poverty because of poor targeting and the benefit taper. Their effectiveness depends most on the size of the rise relative to productivity and on complementary policies. Combining moderate NLW rises with targeted transfers for families with children, such as removing the two-child limit, and more affordable housing would reduce relative poverty more effectively than relying on the wage floor alone.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge: precise definitions of the NLW and relative poverty, including household-level measurement. Application: current NLW level, UC taper, in-work poverty statistic and employer NI rise. Analysis: developed chains on direct pay effects, spillovers, targeting, the taper and employment effects, with reference to the labour market diagram. Evaluation: weighs targeting, the taper, monopsony evidence and the behaviour of the median, then reaches a justified judgement on the conditions under which the policy works, which is Level 3 evaluation.

check.q: All household incomes in a country rise by 8% in real terms and the distribution is otherwise unchanged. What happens to poverty?
options: Both absolute and relative poverty fall
Absolute poverty falls and relative poverty is unchanged
Relative poverty falls and absolute poverty is unchanged
check.explanation: The absolute line is fixed in real terms, so some households rise above it. The relative line is 60% of the median, which also rises by 8%, so the share below it is unchanged.

check.q: Median equivalised household income is £35,000. What is the relative poverty line?
check.explanation: 0.6 × £35,000 = £21,000. Using 50% gives £17,500, a stricter line used in some international comparisons.

check.q: Why are UK relative poverty rates higher after housing costs than before housing costs?
options: Housing benefit is counted as income only in the AHC measure
The AHC measure uses the mean rather than the median
Wealthy households spend a larger share of income on housing
Low-income households spend a larger share of their income on rent
check.explanation: Deducting housing costs reduces poorer households' incomes proportionately more than richer households' incomes, pushing more of them below 60% of the AHC median.

check.q: A Universal Credit claimant pays 20% income tax and 8% NI and UC is withdrawn at 55% of net earnings. What is the effective marginal tax rate?
check.explanation: Of £100 extra, £28 goes in tax and NI; 55% of the remaining £72 (£39.60) is withdrawn. Total £67.60, an EMTR of 67.6%. Adding 55% and 28% double counts.

title: Inequality
overview: Inequality is about how unevenly income and wealth are shared, within a country and between countries. You need to distinguish wealth from income, draw and interpret a Lorenz curve, calculate and interpret a Gini coefficient, explain the causes of inequality, analyse how development changes inequality (the Kuznets curve) and evaluate the significance of capitalism for inequality. Inequality is a favourite 25-mark essay theme on Paper 2 and Paper 3 because it links markets, the labour market, fiscal policy and development.
objectives: Distinguish income from wealth and explain why wealth inequality is greater than income inequality
Draw a Lorenz curve and calculate a Gini coefficient from areas and from quintile data
Explain the causes of income and wealth inequality within and between countries
Analyse the impact of economic change and development on inequality, including the Kuznets curve
Evaluate the significance of capitalism for inequality and whether inequality is harmful or necessary

sections.heading: Income versus wealth
sections.body:
**Income** is a **flow** of money received over a period of time: wages and salaries, rent, interest, dividends, profit and state transfers such as pensions and Universal Credit. **Wealth** is a **stock** of assets owned at a point in time, net of debts: property, pension funds, shares, bonds, savings and physical assets such as businesses.

The two are linked in both directions. Saving out of income builds wealth, and wealth generates income (rent, dividends, interest). Wealth can also be inherited, which is why it transmits advantage across generations.

**Wealth inequality is much greater than income inequality.** In the UK the Gini coefficient for household disposable income is roughly 0.33, while the Gini for total household wealth is around 0.6. ONS data suggest the wealthiest tenth of households hold over 40% of total wealth while the least wealthy half hold under a tenth. Reasons:
- Low-income households have little or no capacity to save; many have negative net wealth (debts exceed assets).
- Returns compound: wealthy households earn income from assets and reinvest it.
- Asset price rises (house prices, equities) benefit those who already own assets; very low interest rates and quantitative easing after 2009 boosted asset prices.
- Inheritance and lifetime gifts pass wealth down, and the UK's housing wealth is heavily concentrated among older owner-occupiers.
- Pension wealth accumulates with age, so wealth inequality also has a strong age dimension.

Exam point: a question about inequality may refer to either measure. Policies that reduce income inequality (progressive income tax, benefits) may leave wealth inequality untouched, which is why some economists argue for reform of property, inheritance and capital gains taxes.

sections.heading: The Lorenz curve
sections.body:
A **Lorenz curve** plots the cumulative percentage of population (ranked from poorest to richest) on the horizontal axis against the cumulative percentage of income (or wealth) they receive on the vertical axis.

- The **line of perfect equality** is the 45-degree diagonal: the poorest 20% receive 20% of income, the poorest 60% receive 60%, and so on.
- An actual Lorenz curve lies below the diagonal and bows towards the bottom right. The further it bows away, the greater the inequality.
- Every Lorenz curve starts at (0, 0) and ends at (100%, 100%), and it is always convex: each additional slice of the population is richer than the last, so the slope increases.

To draw one from data, convert shares into cumulative shares. If quintile shares are 5%, 10%, 15%, 25% and 45%, the cumulative values are 5%, 15%, 30%, 55% and 100%, plotted at 20%, 40%, 60%, 80% and 100% of the population. Read the diagram carefully: a point at (60%, 30%) means the poorest 60% receive 30% of income, so the richest 40% receive 70%.

Comparisons: a Lorenz curve that lies entirely inside another shows unambiguously lower inequality. If two curves cross, the ranking is ambiguous; one country might have a poorer bottom decile but a smaller top share, and a single summary statistic such as the Gini hides this.

Before and after policy: the Lorenz curve for **original income** (market income before taxes and benefits) lies well outside the curve for **disposable income**. In the UK, cash benefits do most of the equalising, with direct taxes adding a smaller effect; indirect taxes such as VAT are regressive and push the other way.

sections.heading: The Gini coefficient
sections.body:
The **Gini coefficient** summarises the Lorenz curve in a single number:

Gini = A ÷ (A + B)

where A is the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve, and B is the area under the Lorenz curve. Because A + B is the triangle under the diagonal (half the unit square, so 0.5 when both axes run from 0 to 1), the formula simplifies to Gini = 2A = 1 − 2B.

- Gini = 0: perfect equality (the Lorenz curve is the diagonal, A = 0).
- Gini = 1: perfect inequality (one person has all the income, B = 0).
- It is often expressed as an index from 0 to 100.

**Calculating from quintile data.** Using the shares above (cumulative 0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.55, 1.00), split B into five trapezia each 0.2 wide. Area = width × (left height + right height) ÷ 2:
- 0.2 × (0 + 0.05) ÷ 2 = 0.005
- 0.2 × (0.05 + 0.15) ÷ 2 = 0.020
- 0.2 × (0.15 + 0.30) ÷ 2 = 0.045
- 0.2 × (0.30 + 0.55) ÷ 2 = 0.085
- 0.2 × (0.55 + 1.00) ÷ 2 = 0.155
B = 0.310, so A = 0.5 − 0.310 = 0.190 and Gini = 0.190 ÷ 0.5 = **0.38**.

Typical values for disposable income: Nordic countries around 0.25 to 0.28; the UK around 0.32 to 0.35; the USA around 0.39 to 0.41; Brazil above 0.5; South Africa around 0.63, among the highest in the world.

**Other measures.** The **20:20 ratio** (income share of the top fifth divided by the bottom fifth; 45 ÷ 5 = 9 in the example) and the **Palma ratio** (top 10% share ÷ bottom 40% share) focus on the tails, where most change in inequality actually happens. The Gini is most sensitive to changes in the middle of the distribution.

Limitations of the Gini: different distributions can give the same Gini; it says nothing about absolute living standards; it depends on whether it is measured for individuals or households, before or after taxes and housing costs; and survey data under-record top incomes.

sections.heading: Causes of inequality within countries
sections.body:
- **Differences in human capital and wages.** Labour markets reward skills that are scarce relative to demand. Graduates and workers with high-demand skills earn more (Theme 3 wage determination).
- **Skill-biased technological change.** Computers and automation complement high-skill work and replace routine middle-skill jobs, widening wage gaps and hollowing out the middle of the distribution.
- **Globalisation.** Competition from lower-wage economies has reduced demand for low-skilled manufacturing labour in advanced economies, while raising returns to capital and to globally mobile talent.
- **Decline of trade unions and changes in labour market institutions.** Lower union membership weakens the bargaining power of lower and middle earners.
- **The tax and benefit system.** Cuts to top income tax rates in the 1980s and less generous benefits contributed to the sharp rise in UK income inequality in that decade, when the Gini rose from around 0.25 to around 0.34. It has been broadly stable since the early 1990s.
- **Wealth and returns to capital.** Owners of capital receive rent, profit and capital gains; if the return on capital exceeds the growth rate of the economy, wealth concentrates over time, a mechanism emphasised by Thomas Piketty.
- **Inheritance and family background.** Unequal starting points in wealth, education and networks reduce social mobility.
- **Household composition and labour market status.** Unemployment, part-time work, single-earner households and disability all reduce income.
- **Discrimination and regional disparities.** Gender and ethnic pay gaps and differences between London and other regions add to inequality.

**Between countries**, inequality reflects differences in productivity, capital per worker, technology, institutions, geography, natural resources, historical factors such as colonialism, and access to global markets and finance.

sections.heading: Economic change, development and the Kuznets curve
sections.body:
Simon Kuznets suggested an inverted-U relationship between GDP per capita and inequality. In early development most people work in low-productivity agriculture with similar low incomes, so inequality is low. As industrialisation begins, a minority move into higher-paid urban jobs and owners of capital earn high returns, so inequality rises. Later, as most of the workforce moves into the modern sector, education spreads, wages rise, workers organise and states build progressive tax and welfare systems, so inequality falls.

Evidence is mixed. Inequality rose in China during its rapid industrialisation from the 1980s to around 2008 and has since stabilised or fallen slightly, consistent with the rising part of the curve. But many advanced economies, including the UK and the USA, saw inequality rise again from the 1980s, which the simple Kuznets story does not predict. Latin American countries are highly unequal at middle-income levels largely because of historical land ownership patterns and institutions, not just their stage of development.

**Global inequality** (between all individuals in the world) has fallen since around 1990, mainly because China and India grew faster than rich countries, even though inequality within many countries rose. This distinction between within-country and between-country inequality earns credit.

sections.heading: Capitalism and inequality: necessary, harmful or both?
sections.body:
Capitalism allocates resources through private ownership, markets and the profit motive. It tends to generate inequality because:
- returns go to owners of scarce factors, and capital is owned unequally;
- competition creates winners and losers, and network effects create 'winner-takes-most' markets (large tech platforms);
- unequal outcomes can become unequal opportunities through inheritance and education.

**Arguments that some inequality is beneficial:** unequal rewards create incentives to work, train, take risks and innovate; profits signal where resources are wanted and finance investment; higher earners save more, funding investment. Free market economists argue the focus should be absolute poverty, not inequality, and that growth is a 'rising tide'.

**Arguments that high inequality is harmful:**
- **Lower aggregate demand.** Lower-income households have a higher marginal propensity to consume, so concentrating income at the top can depress consumption.
- **Lower social mobility and wasted talent.** Countries with higher inequality tend to have lower intergenerational mobility (the 'Great Gatsby curve'), so able children from poor backgrounds under-invest in education.
- **Social and health costs.** Inequality is associated with worse health, crime and lower trust, raising government spending.
- **Political capture and instability.** Concentrated wealth can influence policy in favour of the rich, and resentment fuels instability.
- **Less durable growth.** IMF research has found that higher inequality is associated with shorter spells of growth.

Capitalism is not a single system: Nordic social-market economies combine markets with high taxes, strong unions and universal services and have Gini coefficients around 0.25, whereas the more liberal US model has a Gini near 0.4. So the significance of capitalism for inequality depends heavily on the institutions that accompany it.

key_terms.definition: A flow of money received over a period, from wages, rent, interest, profit, dividends and state transfers.
A stock of assets owned at a point in time, such as property, shares, pensions and savings, net of debts.
A curve showing the cumulative share of income or wealth received by the cumulative share of the population, ranked from poorest to richest.
The 45-degree line on a Lorenz diagram, showing every x% of the population receiving x% of income.

A measure of inequality equal to the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve divided by the total area under the line of equality; ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality).
The income share of the richest 10% divided by the income share of the poorest 40%.
Household income from the market (employment, investments, private pensions) before any state taxes and benefits.
Income after direct taxes have been deducted and cash benefits added.
A hypothesised inverted-U relationship in which inequality first rises and then falls as GDP per capita increases.
Technological progress that raises the productivity and demand for skilled workers relative to less skilled workers, widening wage differentials.
The ability of individuals to move between income or social groups, especially relative to their parents.
An economic system based on private ownership of the means of production, markets and the pursuit of profit.

diagrams.title: Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient
diagrams.caption: Built from quintile shares of 5, 10, 15, 25 and 45%. Area B under the curve is 0.31 of the unit square, area A is 0.19, so Gini = A ÷ (A + B) = 0.19 ÷ 0.5 = 0.38.

diagrams.title: Taxes and benefits shift the Lorenz curve towards equality
diagrams.caption: The original income curve (Gini 0.5) bows further from the diagonal than the disposable income curve (Gini about 0.33), similar to the UK pattern. Cash benefits and progressive income tax move the curve towards the line of equality.

diagrams.title: The Kuznets curve
diagrams.caption: Inequality rises as a minority move from low-productivity agriculture into high-paid modern-sector jobs, then falls as the modern sector absorbs most workers and the state redistributes. Rising inequality in rich economies since the 1980s challenges the right-hand side of the curve.

formulae.name: Gini coefficient
formulae.formula: Gini = A ÷ (A + B) = 1 − 2B (with both axes running 0 to 1)

formulae.name: Area of each trapezium under the Lorenz curve
formulae.formula: width × (cumulative share at start + cumulative share at end) ÷ 2

formulae.name: 20:20 ratio
formulae.formula: income share of richest 20% ÷ income share of poorest 20%
formulae.example: 45% ÷ 5% = 9: the richest fifth receive nine times as much as the poorest fifth.

formulae.name: Palma ratio
formulae.formula: income share of richest 10% ÷ income share of poorest 40%
formulae.example: If the top 10% receive 30% and the bottom 40% receive 20%, Palma = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5.

applications: UK income and wealth: the Gini for UK disposable income has been roughly 0.32 to 0.35 since the early 1990s after rising sharply in the 1980s. The Gini for original income is much higher, around 0.5, showing the redistributive effect of benefits and direct taxes. Wealth is far more unequal, with a Gini around 0.6, and the wealthiest tenth of households hold over 40% of total wealth according to ONS estimates.

Quantitative easing and asset prices: Bank of England QE from 2009 to 2021 lowered long-term interest rates and raised asset prices. This supported jobs and incomes across the economy, but holders of shares and property gained most in wealth terms, which critics argue widened wealth inequality, particularly between older homeowners and younger renters.

South Africa and Brazil: South Africa's Gini of around 0.63 reflects the legacy of apartheid in land, education and labour markets, high unemployment and a large gap between formal and informal sector earnings. Brazil reduced inequality in the 2000s through rising minimum wages and the Bolsa Família cash-transfer programme, though its Gini remains above 0.5.

China's development: inequality rose sharply during industrialisation and urbanisation from the 1980s, with large gaps between coastal cities and rural inland provinces and between urban workers and rural migrants, broadly consistent with the rising part of the Kuznets curve.

Nordic model: Denmark, Norway, Finland and Sweden combine market economies with high taxes, universal services and strong collective bargaining. Disposable income Ginis around 0.25 to 0.28 show that capitalism does not have a single inevitable level of inequality.
evaluation: Income or wealth? Wealth inequality is much greater and more persistent; a judgement about whether inequality is rising should specify which.

Inequality versus poverty: rising inequality can coincide with falling absolute poverty when everyone gets richer but the top gains most; a top answer considers which matters more for welfare and why.

Some inequality is efficient because it rewards effort, skill and risk, but beyond some point it reduces aggregate demand, social mobility and the durability of growth; the issue is the degree and the source of inequality (effort versus inheritance or rent-seeking).
Measurement: the Gini hides where in the distribution change occurs and survey data under-record top incomes, so the Palma ratio or top 1% share may tell a different story.

Institutions matter more than the system label: capitalist economies with strong redistribution and universal education have much lower inequality, so capitalism is a necessary but not sufficient explanation.

Time frame: the Kuznets curve suggests inequality may rise temporarily during development, so short-run increases may not be permanent, but evidence from rich countries since the 1980s shows a fall is not automatic.
misconceptions: A Gini of 0.6 means the richest 60% hold everything. The Gini is a ratio of areas; it does not directly read off any population share.
Income and wealth are interchangeable. Income is a flow; wealth is a stock. Wealth inequality is much greater.
A Lorenz curve further from the diagonal shows more equality. It shows more inequality; the closer to the diagonal, the more equal.
All taxes reduce inequality. Indirect taxes like VAT are regressive, taking a larger share of income from poorer households.
If two Lorenz curves cross, the one with the lower Gini is unambiguously more equal. When curves cross the ranking depends on which part of the distribution you care about.
exam_tips: Label a Lorenz diagram fully: both axes as cumulative percentages, the line of equality, the Lorenz curve, and areas A and B; then state Gini = A ÷ (A + B).
In data questions you may be asked to plot cumulative shares or comment on a change in the Gini; always quantify (for example, from 0.34 to 0.36, a 0.02 rise) and interpret what it means.
Use synoptic links: wage determination and labour market failure (Theme 3), progressive taxation (4.5.2), QE (4.4.3 and 2.6.2), development (4.3).
In a 25-mark essay on capitalism and inequality, contrast different models of capitalism (US, UK, Nordic) and weigh efficiency arguments against the costs of inequality to reach a judgement.
Distinguish within-country from between-country and global inequality; they can move in opposite directions.

model_answer.question: Evaluate the view that a capitalist economic system inevitably leads to increasing inequality of income and wealth.
model_answer.answer:
Capitalism is an economic system in which most resources are privately owned and allocated through markets in pursuit of profit. Inequality refers to the uneven distribution of income, a flow of earnings over time, and wealth, a stock of assets at a point in time. It is usually measured by the Gini coefficient, the ratio of the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve to the total area under the line of equality.

There are strong reasons why capitalism generates inequality. First, in a market economy factor incomes reflect the scarcity and productivity of the factors people own. Workers with scarce skills face high demand and inelastic supply, so their wages are high, while low-skilled workers face elastic supply and low wages. Technological change has been skill-biased: digital technology complements graduates and replaces routine middle-skilled jobs, so the wage gap widens and the Lorenz curve bows further from the diagonal.

Second, capital is unequally owned, and capitalism rewards ownership. Owners of capital receive profits, dividends, rent and capital gains. If the rate of return on capital exceeds the growth rate of the economy, as Piketty argued has been the normal historical pattern, wealth grows faster than incomes and becomes increasingly concentrated, especially when passed on through inheritance. This explains why UK wealth inequality, with a Gini of around 0.6, is far higher than income inequality, around 0.33. Policy reinforced this after 2009: quantitative easing lowered interest rates and raised house and share prices, benefiting existing asset owners most.

Third, competition creates winners. In markets with network effects and economies of scale, such as digital platforms, a few firms capture most of the market, and their founders and shareholders receive very large returns. Globalisation has added to this by expanding markets for successful firms and highly mobile workers, while exposing low-skilled workers in advanced economies to import competition. Finally, unequal outcomes become unequal opportunities: children from wealthy families get better education and networks, so inequality persists across generations, a pattern shown by the Great Gatsby curve.

However, the word inevitably is too strong. The evidence shows enormous variation in inequality among capitalist economies. Nordic countries are capitalist, with private ownership, open trade and large global firms, yet have disposable income Ginis around 0.25 to 0.28 because of progressive taxes, universal childcare and education, and strong collective bargaining. The USA has a Gini near 0.4. The difference lies in institutions, not in the existence of capitalism. Similarly, the UK's Gini for original income is around 0.5 but falls to about 0.33 after taxes and benefits: the state can offset much market inequality.

Second, inequality has not increased continuously. In the UK income inequality rose sharply in the 1980s, driven by deindustrialisation, the decline of unions and cuts to top tax rates, but has been broadly flat since the early 1990s. Kuznets argued that inequality rises during industrialisation and then falls as the modern sector absorbs most workers and education spreads; China's inequality rose during rapid industrialisation and has since stabilised. Inequality between countries has fallen since around 1990 as China and India have grown faster than rich economies, so capitalism and globalisation have reduced global inequality while raising it within some countries.

Third, capitalism has also cut absolute poverty dramatically. Market reforms in China after 1978 lifted hundreds of millions out of extreme poverty. Even if relative inequality rose, the poorest became much better off, and some inequality is necessary for incentives to invest, innovate and acquire skills.

That said, wealth inequality is more likely to rise under capitalism than income inequality, because it compounds and is less directly affected by the tax and benefit system. Many countries tax income from work more heavily than income from wealth, and capital is internationally mobile, which makes wealth harder to tax. So without deliberate policy, the tendency is towards rising wealth concentration.

In conclusion, capitalism creates powerful forces towards inequality through unequal factor ownership, skill-biased technology and winner-takes-most markets, and these are strongest for wealth. But increasing inequality is not inevitable: it depends on institutions and policy choices, such as progressive taxation, investment in education, labour market institutions and the taxation of wealth and inheritance. The more mobile capital becomes, the harder these policies are to sustain, so the risk of rising wealth inequality is greatest where governments do not cooperate internationally on taxation.
model_answer.commentary: Knowledge and application: precise definitions of capitalism, income, wealth and the Gini; UK, US, Nordic and Chinese evidence with approximate figures. Analysis: several developed chains (factor scarcity and skill-biased technology, returns to capital and compounding, winner-takes-most markets, intergenerational transmission) with Lorenz curve reasoning. Evaluation: challenges 'inevitably' using variation between capitalist economies, the role of redistribution, time trends, the Kuznets curve and global versus national inequality, then distinguishes income from wealth to reach a nuanced, justified judgement. This meets Level 4 KAA and Level 3 evaluation.

check.explanation: Wealth, such as shares and property, is a stock measured at a point in time; the others are flows of income.

options: some workers move from low-productivity agriculture into higher-paid modern-sector jobs
the share of the workforce in agriculture rises
